deep.reconstruction:
Grothendieck sets up the theory of pseudoline arrangements inside his own language of 'cartes' (maps: topological or combinatorial cellular embeddings of a graph in a surface).

(1) Definition. A system of pseudolines is a map whose underlying surface X is a real projective plane. His marginal note characterises this as a compact non-orientable surface of Euler–Poincaré characteristic 1. Every vertex has even degree at least 4. Even degree lets one continue 'straight through' each vertex (opposite edges in the cyclic order). This partitions the edges into equivalence classes, called the pseudolines of the map. The axiom is that any two pseudolines meet in exactly one point.

(2) First consequences.
- The number n of pseudolines is at least 2.
- He wrote 'L'immersion' (the transcription has 'inversion'). The immersion S^1 → P^2_R given by a pseudoline lies in the non-nullhomotopic class of the two possible isotopy classes. Equivalently, X is non-orientable along it (a one-sided curve, i.e. a Möbius-band neighbourhood), exactly as for a projective line. The reason: two curves meeting transversally in exactly one point have Z/2 intersection number 1, so neither is null-homologous.
- He quotes the known stretchability fact: simple arrangements (all vertices of degree 4) with n ≤ 6 are realisable by actual lines in P^2_R.

(3) Orientation double cover. Let D be a pseudoline and X~ the orientation double cover of X; X~ is S^2, which he identifies with P^1_C. Let D~ be the preimage of D (written 'dans X', a slip for X~). Because D is one-sided, D~ is a single connected circle, a 'great pseudocircle'. So X~ \ D~ has two components, the 'hemispheres'. These are in canonical bijection with the two orientations of D. Concretely:
- X \ D is an open disc, and each hemisphere maps homeomorphically onto it.
- Each hemisphere carries the tautological local orientation of X, i.e. an orientation of the disc.
- The induced boundary orientation on the boundary circle, which double-covers D, descends to D, since the deck rotation preserves orientation.

The page breaks off with 'Notons que l'ens. des sommets se trouvant…'. The next page continues: the vertices on D give D an induced polygon structure, and the set of hemispheres π_0(X~ \ D~) matches the orientations of that polygon. For a vertex s and a pseudoline D not through s, the local orientations of X at s, Ω_s(X), are in bijection with Ω(D). He then asks how to make the composite bijection Ω(D) → Ω_s(X) → Ω(D') explicit, using two pseudolines through s.

The purpose is a purely combinatorial ('in terms of the 1-complex K^1 and its decomposition into pseudolines') account of the orientation and sign structure of an arrangement. This is essentially rediscovering the covector/chirotope data of a rank-3 oriented matroid from the map.
errors: 'D~ l'image inverse de D dans X' should read 'dans X~' (slip of the pen).

The definition implicitly needs each pseudoline class to be a simple closed curve, i.e. not passing twice through a vertex. This is not stated explicitly, though it partly follows from the intersection axiom only if one also forbids self-crossings.

The stretchability bound n ≤ 6 is correct but weaker than what was known by then. Goodman–Pollack (1980) showed every arrangement of at most 8 pseudolines is stretchable; the first non-stretchable simple arrangement has 9 (Ringel's non-Pappus configuration).

ideas.what: Pseudoline arrangement defined as a map on RP^2 with even vertex degrees ≥4, pseudolines obtained as 'straight-through' edge classes, pairwise meeting exactly once
ideas.modern_name: (projective) arrangement of pseudolines / its cell-complex (map) description
ideas.usually_credited_to: Levi (1926); Ringel (1956); Grünbaum, 'Arrangements and Spreads' (1972); Goodman–Pollack

ideas.what: Each pseudoline is an essential, one-sided curve in RP^2
ideas.modern_name: pseudolines are non-separating, non-contractible simple closed curves

ideas.what: Simple arrangements of ≤6 pseudolines are stretchable
Lifting to the orientation double cover S^2; complement of the lifted pseudoline has two hemispheres canonically indexed by the orientations of D
ideas.modern_name: centrally symmetric pseudocircle arrangement on S^2; topological representation of rank-3 oriented matroids (signed covectors)

missed.claim: Writing X~ ≅ S^2 ≅ P^1_C puts pseudoline arrangements into the setting of maps on the Riemann sphere carrying a fixed-point-free orientation-reversing involution. In effect these are 'real' maps/dessins in the sense of his dessins-d'enfants programme. Little literature treats pseudoline arrangements as antiholomorphic-symmetric dessins on P^1_C. The identification is only hinted at here, not developed.
missed.quote: X~ le revêtement des orientations de X (X~ ≃ S^2 ≃ P^1_C)
missed.why_it_might_matter_today: It could link oriented-matroid realisability (stretchability) questions with Belyi/real-dessin theory and Galois actions on maps. This is speculative, and nothing on this page develops it.

deep.surprise_reason: The page is an introductory restatement of standard pseudoline-arrangement facts (Levi, Grünbaum, Folkman–Lawrence) in Grothendieck's map language. The stretchability bound he quotes is weaker than what was known. Only the P^1_C identification faintly hints at a dessins connection.
transcription_corrections: 'L'inversion [?] de S^1 dans P^2_R' should read 'L'immersion de S^1 dans P^2_R'.
'le nb {+n+} des pseudodroites' – the n is an interlinear insertion above 'des' (an 'ensemble/nombre n'); the reading is fine.
Margin: 'i.e. (compacte) non orientable de car. EP égale à 1…' – confirmed.
'D~ l'image inverse de D dans X' faithfully reflects the manuscript; the mathematical intent is X~.
Last line: the interlinear word above 'l'' appears to be 'sur' (as in 'l'ens. des sommets se trouvant sur une même D'), not 'sing'.
